title: Optical spectroscopy of Bose-Einstein condensates at finite temperature
authors: R. M. F. Andersen, L. N. Stokholm, I. Zebergs, N. R. Neubert, A. S. Chatterley, N. Kjærgaard, J. J. Arlt
abstract: We report on optical spectroscopic measurements of ultracold and partially condensed 87Rb gases, which show distinct spectral features due to the thermal and the Bose condensed components in the frequency domain. These features are detected in-situ by using a dark-field configuration with single-photon sensitivity and a frequency-agile laser system. To interpret the observed spectra, we develop a model for light propagation through an inhomogeneous atomic cloud. This model enables the extraction of temperature and atom number, which we benchmark against conventional time-of-flight absorption imaging. The spectroscopically obtained cloud parameters show enhanced sensitivity to small thermal fractions in nearly pure condensates. We further compare the spectroscopy in dark-field and bright-field configurations, demonstrating the superior performance of the former. Our results reveal previously unexplored spectral structure in optically dense ultracold gases and establish spectroscopy as a tool for characterizing ultracold systems at very low temperatures.
summary: The research reports on using optical spectroscopy to characterize ultracold Bose-Einstein condensates of $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms. By measuring spectral features in both dark-field and bright-field configurations, the authors developed a model to extract temperature and atom numbers directly within the trap. The findings establish that dark-field spectroscopy is a highly sensitive and superior tool for characterizing these quantum gases at very low temperatures.
main_problem: The study aims to characterize ultracold, partially condensed atomic gases by measuring distinct spectral features arising from both thermal and Bose-Einstein condensed components.
main_result: Dark-field optical spectroscopy proves to be a superior technique compared to bright-field measurements for characterizing these systems, showing good agreement with Time-of-Flight imaging for temperature and atom numbers.
method: The experiment uses an in-situ dark-field configuration with single-photon detection and a frequency-agile laser system to measure spectral profiles as a function of probe detuning.
model_or_system: The physical system is a cloud of $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms trapped in a crossed optical dipole trap. The analysis relies on developing a model for light propagation through this inhomogeneous atomic cloud, incorporating density components ($ho = ho_0 + ho_{th}$).
key_observables: Spectral features (intensity profiles) measured as a function of probe frequency detuning ($\delta$); extracted parameters include temperature ($T$), thermal atom number ($N_{th}$), and condensed atom number ($N_0$).
important_parameters: Low temperatures (nK range); the ratio between thermal and condensed fractions; spectral detuning ($\delta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a thin-lens approximation for light propagation, which is noted as a potential source of systematic deviation in cold spectra.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup (schematics), simulated BF and DF spectra for partially condensed clouds, and comparisons between spectroscopically derived parameters and those from TOF absorption imaging.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first detailing the measurement setup and spectral diagnostics in both dark-field and bright-field configurations. It then develops the theoretical model for light propagation through the inhomogeneous cloud, followed by a detailed comparison of results against conventional Time-of-Flight measurements to validate the spectroscopic technique.
why_interesting: This work provides an advanced, non-destructive, in-situ diagnostic tool for characterizing quantum gas mixtures at extremely low temperatures, offering quantitative metrics (T, $N_{th}$, $N_0$) that complement traditional time-of-flight methods.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Schematic of the detection setup. Collimated probe light (orange) is sent through a cloud of trapped atoms, and some of the light is scattered (blue). At the focus plane of the probe beam, an optional small dark-field obstacle can be placed to block only the unscattered light. Additional filtering is achieved by a pinhole at an intermediate image plane. The image is either relayed onto a camera or focused onto a single-photon detector (SPD).
